              III.   DISTRIBUTION INVESTMENT IN NEW MEXICO

 1   Q.   Are there increasing demands and expectations on the distribution system?

 2   A.   Yes. SPS is facing significant load growth as individuals and businesses look to

 3        the electric system to serve new requests and to facilitate the decarbonization of

 4        industrial processes, transportation, and heating services, placing additional

 5        requirements on the distribution system. Additionally, exogenous factors, such as

 6        climate-related risks are also driving new expectations and requirements for the

 7        grid from a reliability and resiliency perspective. Taken together, this means that

 8        planning the distribution system must have a more robust and proactive approach

 9        that seeks to achieve multiple objectives through the investments made. There is

10        uncertainty that comes with new sources of demand, and a range of possibilities

11        must be considered for projected load alongside customer requests. Currently, the

12        largest factor contributing to the growth of the distribution system in New Mexico

13        is the oil and gas-related growth from both additional exploration and more recently

14        efforts to electrify oil and gas production processes.

 1   Q.   How has SPS undertaken distribution planning activities historically?

 2   A.   Historically, distribution planning efforts have primarily consisted of investing in

 3        new infrastructure to serve requested load growth and investing in asset health and

 4        reliability to ensure that infrastructure is maintained and utilized efficiently on the

 5        system. At SPS, distribution planning was historically completed at the local level,

 6        and as issues arose from generic growth or customer requests, projects were created

 7        to address them and installed. This approach was effective when load growth was

 8        slower, more predictable, and project lead times were shorter.

 9   Q.   Are there alternative ways to plan the distribution system that account for

10        increasing system complexities and changing customer needs?

11   A.   Yes. Across the nation, electric customers want to use electricity differently,

12        generate their own electricity, and manage their usage to reduce the cost of their

13        electric bills. Additionally, distributed energy resources, including battery energy

14        storage systems, create two-way flows on the system. These factors add another

15        layer of challenges for preparing the distribution system for a range of possible

16        futures from a load perspective, including potentially changing customer behaviors

17        and adoption of distributed energy resources.          The traditional approach to

18        distribution planning is no longer adequate. As such, Xcel Energy has stood up an

19        enterprise-wide dedicated distribution planning team, including personnel

 2        adoption trends to have the ability to identify projects earlier, which is particularly

 3        important at this juncture given the additional construction leads times facing the

 4        industry. SPS forecasts the need for this distribution planning focus and team to

 5        grow as additional requirements and loads are placed on the distribution system.

 1        IV.       THE RANKING, ESTIMATION, AND MANAGEMENT OF
 2                        DISTRIBUTION CAPITAL ADDITIONS

 3   Q.   Please describe the distribution function and the work that the distribution

 4        business area performs to support SPS’s operations.

 5   A.   The distribution function focuses on reliability, safety, customer service,

 6        operational efficiency, and the fiscal oversight necessary to construct, operate, and

 7        maintain SPS’s electric distribution system in New Mexico and Texas. The

 8        electrical distribution system is an integral part of SPS’s overall operations,

 9        providing the medium voltage backbone, the customer service facilities, and the

10        metering of electrical usage. The distribution function includes the following areas:

11              •    Distribution Business Operations;

12              •    Distribution Electric Engineering;

13              •    Distribution Planning and Strategy;

14              •    Distribution Planning and Performance;

15              •    Customer Delivery;

16              •    Gas Operations;

17              •    Distribution Scheduling;

18              •    Distribution Control Centers; and

19              •    Distribution Operations.

                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                       Casey S. Meeks

 1        Distribution Operations has the primary responsibility in the distribution area,

 2        including siting and land rights, design, work coordination, construction, and

 3        contract and utility services. The other areas provide necessary support functions

 4        such as engineering, scheduling, mapping system maintenance and updates, system

 5        reliability and control, and a number of other roles required for end-to-end

 6        operations.

 7   Q.   How does SPS decide which distribution projects to construct at any given

 8        time?

 9   A.   SPS’s distribution capital expenditures can be divided into two broad categories:

10        mandatory, or non-discretionary, and discretionary. Mandatory projects are those

11        that SPS is required to undertake; either because of its obligation to serve all

12        customers in its New Mexico retail service area or because of the need to preserve

13        the safety and reliability of the distribution system. Discretionary projects are

14        optional investments for which not executing and spending the funds does not

15        imminently endanger SPS employees or the public from a safety or reliability

16        incident on the system. SPS prioritizes the construction of the non-discretionary

17        distribution projects, and then it ranks and prioritizes the discretionary projects in

18        accordance with a process that I outline later in my testimony.


                                               17
                                    Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Casey S. Meeks

 1   Q.   What are some types of non-discretionary distribution projects that SPS is

 2        required to construct?

 3   A.   Non-discretionary distribution projections include things like work required for

 4        SPS to meet its obligation to serve new customers; infrastructure work related to

 5        increasing feeder and substation capacity to deal with equipment overloads,

 6        contingencies, and voltage support; replacement of wood poles that are damaged

 7        by vehicles and the replacement of substation components, such as circuit breakers,

 8        voltage regulators, or lightning arrestors; replacement of failing or damaged

 9        equipment and new installations made at customers’ requests; and replacement of

10        existing outdoor lighting with more reliable and cost-effective Light-Emitting

11        Diode (“LED”) lighting fixtures when requested by customers. Collectively, non-

12        discretionary projects consume most of SPS’s distribution capital budget.

13   Q.   Please turn now to the discretionary distribution capital projects. How does

14        SPS prioritize those projects?

15   A.   The Distribution business area has a well-defined process for identifying, ranking,

16        and approving discretionary distribution capital projects. At a high level, the

17        process of approving capital expenditures begins with completing all the steps

 1        necessary to evaluate the capital expenditures for a project’s life cycle. Identifying

 2        and assessing risks and their related mitigations are central to this process.

 3   Q.   Please describe what you mean when you refer to “risks” and “mitigations.”

 4   A.   Risks are problems that can result in negative consequences to SPS’s customers,

 5        the environment, or SPS’s ability to provide safe and reliable service. Mitigations

 6        are solutions that address the risks. For example, the following lists both a risk and

 7        a possible mitigation for that risk:

 8            Risk:    Overload of 12.5 kilovolt (“kV”) Livingston Ridge Substation
 9                    Transformer
10            Mitigation: Install Livingston Ridge #2 Transformer: 115/12.47, 28 Megavolt-
11                   Amperes (“MVA”)

12   Q.   What is the process for identifying and ranking the discretionary distribution

13        capital projects?

14   A.   SPS follows the nine-step process listed below to identify and rank discretionary

15        distribution capital projects.

16            Step 1 - SPS engineering and operations employees identify potential risks and
17                     mitigations, the estimated life of the project, the associated costs, and
18                     the estimated in-service date.

19            Step 2 - SPS then reviews each risk and mitigation for accuracy, completeness,
20                     and reasonableness.




                                                 19
                                     Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                       Casey S. Meeks

1            Step 3 - SPS next scores risks and mitigations based on certain criteria such as
2                     the likelihood of the risk occurring and the consequences of failing to
3                     address the risk.

4            Step 4 - SPS then ranks all risks and mitigations by priority.

5            Step 5 - The business area determines which risks/mitigations will be funded
6                     during the year.

7            Step 6 - Risks and mitigations are assigned a capital work structure based on
8                     the type of work involved. Capital projects are classified either as
9                     “discrete” or “blanket.”

10           Step 7 - In-service dates are projected for large, “discrete” capital projects.
11                    “Blanket” work structures are placed in-service based on monthly
12                    closing patterns.

13           Step 8 - SPS then reviews and approves all capital projects that are included
14                    within the authorized funding level.

15           Step 9 - Approved projects are constructed during the year.

16   Q.   Please describe how engineering and operations personnel estimate the costs

17        of proposed capital projects during Step No. 1.

18   A.   Engineering and Operations personnel estimate costs of proposed projects based on

19        historical actual costs of projects with similar scope and scale. Those estimates, of

20        course, must account for any differences between the historical and proposed

21        projects, and they must account for other factors such as increases in the price of

22        materials.

 1   Q.      In Step No. 6, you refer to the assignment of work structures. Please describe

 2           how SPS assigns work structures. 2

 3   A.      When a mitigation becomes an approved project, SPS may assign it a unique

 4           tracking number based on a dollar threshold. If the project cost exceeds $250,000,

 5           it is generally considered a “discrete” project, and it is assigned a unique work

 6           structure number for purposes of tracking and reporting.

 7                    If a project cost is less than $250,000, it is typically considered a routine

 8           project whose cost is tracked and recorded under a “blanket” work structure number

 9           that includes many other small projects. For example, all new overhead service-

 3   Q.   What changes is SPS proposing to Rule No. 16?

 4   A.   SPS is proposing updates to the line extension policy to better align with modern

 5        infrastructure needs, improve coordination with third-party vendors, enhance

 6        wildfire mitigation efforts, and ensure equitable cost distribution.

 7   Q.   Why is SPS proposing these changes?

 8   A.   These changes address two key areas: underground trenching construction

 9        allowance inclusion and clarifications around wildfire risk mitigation through

10        underground line extensions.

11   Q.   What is the issue with underground trenching costs under the current policy?

12   A.   Currently, underground trenching and ditching costs outside of subdivisions or

13        developer-funded projects are excluded from the construction allowance. This

14        often leads to delays, cost disputes, and quality concerns when customers must

15        coordinate trenching independently. Including these costs within the allowance

16        will streamline project execution, improve vendor coordination, and generally

17        reduce the financial burden to customers when adequate construction allowance is

18        available.

 3   A.   Tier 2 and Tier 3 wildfire zones are areas identified as having elevated or extreme

 8   A.   To mitigate wildfire risk, SPS proposes requiring underground installation of

10        SPS. Undergrounding reduces ignition sources and enhances system resilience.

11        This approach ensures that those in high-risk areas bear the cost of mitigation,

12        rather than distributing it across all ratepayers.

16        risk and long-term maintenance costs. It also prevents the financial burden of

17        mitigation from being unfairly shared by customers in lower-risk areas.
